name: Clean Email
tagline: Bulk email cleanup, unsubscribe, automation, and privacy controls

pricing.basis: paid plan; billing basis requires review
pricing.native: Public paid plan exists; amount not safely recovered
pricing.notes: The official pricing URL is recorded, but a stable current amount was not safely recoverable in this pass. Do not publish a number until rechecked.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Clean up to 1,000 messages; unsubscribe from 25 subscriptions; no Auto Clean, Screener, or premium sender/list settings
tiers.notes: A separate 14-day premium trial enables unlimited cleaning and all premium features without a card; it includes 25 unsubscribe actions.

tiers.name: Premium, 1 account
tiers.limits: 1 email account; unlimited email cleaning; all current and future features

tiers.name: Premium, 5 accounts
tiers.limits: 5 email accounts; unlimited email cleaning; all current and future features
tiers.notes: Annual total is $49.99; accounts can be shared with friends or family.

tiers.name: Premium, 10 accounts
tiers.limits: 10 email accounts; unlimited email cleaning; all current and future features
tiers.notes: Annual total is $99.99; accounts can be shared with friends or family.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Clean up to 1,000 messages and unsubscribe from 25 subscriptions; premium-only automation/settings excluded; optional 14-day premium trial
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; annual plans save up to 70%; cancel or change plan at any time
pricing.hiddenCosts: Pricing jumps by mailbox bundle: managing more than 1 account requires the 5-account plan, and more than 5 requires the 10-account plan.

verdictSummary: The visible inbox cleanup loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Clean Email earns its keep through deliverability, security, integration, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local email companion for inbox cleanup that works on exported mail or one user-authorized IMAP account.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: IMAP or Gmail OAuth credentials where supported
whatYouLose: sender reputation, deliverability, and suppression handling
team routing and shared inbox rules
whyPeopleStillPay: Clean Email: Email is infrastructure. Customers pay to avoid lost messages, broken auth, spam problems, and the reputational cost of a flaky inbox.
ongoingBurden: Own OAuth refresh, IMAP quirks, encryption, spam handling, notification delivery, and provider policy changes.

priorArt.name: Mailspring
priorArt.desc: Open-source desktop mail client and useful IMAP prior art.

alternatives.name: Edison Mail
alternatives.desc: Bulk delete, unsubscribe, rules and sender blocking for free; opt out of the shopping-data research if that sentence bothered you.

facts.install: Install the desktop or mobile app and add existing email accounts
facts.engines: Edison’s proprietary AI-based Assistant/search and smart-folder system; the model or backend is not disclosed on the checked official pages
facts.dataFormat: Messages remain with the mailbox provider and are cached in the client; Edison also processes account and message-derived data through its services, with separate controls for optional commerce-research participation
facts.gapVsPaid: Edison can unsubscribe and block senders inside its client, but it lacks Clean Email’s provider-agnostic background Auto Clean rules, Screener, and auditable cleanup history.

alternatives.name: Gmailytics
alternatives.desc: Gmail cleanup by sender with unlimited unsubscribes; background automation and other mail providers stayed home.

facts.install: Sign in to the hosted service with Google OAuth and grant Gmail access
facts.dataFormat: Gmail messages stay in Google; Gmailytics says it reads metadata rather than bodies, subjects, or attachments, and stores account details, cleanup history, aggregate statistics, and limited sender/date/size/category/unsubscribe metadata
facts.gapVsPaid: Gmailytics is Gmail-only, caps free cleanup at 2,000 messages per 30 days, and lacks Clean Email’s continuous Auto Clean rules, Screener, and Read Later workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: Gmail only, and setup requires granting Google OAuth permissions

alternatives.name: Inbox Zero
alternatives.desc: Rules, bulk unsubscribe, cold-email blocking and cleanup under your own roof; OAuth and Docker are the cover charge.

facts.install: Use the hosted service or run the official CLI-assisted Docker deployment with Node.js, PostgreSQL, Redis, OAuth, and environment variables
facts.engines: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, Groq, and OpenRouter, selected through configuration
facts.dataFormat: Account, rule, and encrypted OAuth-token metadata live in PostgreSQL and Redis on the selected host; email content used for classification can be sent to the configured model provider
facts.gapVsPaid: Inbox Zero’s free route demands Docker, OAuth infrastructure, and an AI key and supports a narrower mailbox set than Clean Email’s zero-admin multi-provider service.
facts.setupBlocker: The free self-hosted path needs Docker, Node.js 24+, Google or Microsoft OAuth application setup, mail webhooks or Pub/Sub, a domain with TLS, and an AI API key

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cleanfox
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free and functional, but market research on anonymized inbox data is still the business model.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Gmail Cleaner
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free and local, but setup starts by creating a Google Cloud OAuth app; that is not a non-builder install.

rejectedAlternatives.name: InboxPurge
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The local extension works, but twenty free actions barely clears one afternoon's backlog.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Clean Email is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Clean Email, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Tauri 2 + React + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local email companion for inbox cleanup that works on exported mail or one user-authorized IMAP account.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: sender reputation, deliverability, and suppression handling; provider-grade deliverability; push reliability across devices.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
